opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think the short answer is that we don't fully know yet, but there are some suggestive hints.

One thing we've learned from psycholinguistics is that readers are quite sensitive to the statistics of what they've been exposed to. When you read, you're constantly predicting what's coming next, and those predictions come from your experience. So if you spend a lot of time with academic prose, or legal texts, or nineteenth-century novels with long, heavily embedded sentences, you'd expect your expectations to shift. A structure that's rare and confusing for most readers, like a center-embedded relative clause or a long gap between a subject and its verb, might become less surprising to you, and so less costly to process.

There's some evidence along these lines. People who read more tend to handle certain difficult constructions, like object relative clauses, more easily, and you can even shift people's behavior in the lab by exposing them to many examples of a structure. So at least part of what we call "difficulty" seems to depend on experience, not just fixed limits on memory.

Then there's the question of strategy, which is a bit different. Experienced readers of dense text might learn to read more patiently, holding off on committing to an interpretation, or to go back and reread when something doesn't fit. Someone used to short, simple sentences might be more prone to what's sometimes called "good-enough" processing, building a shallow interpretation that's plausible but doesn't fully reflect the syntax.

Cross-linguistically it gets even more interesting. Speakers of verb-final languages like Japanese or German routinely have to hold several arguments in memory before the verb arrives, and there's some suggestion that they're better at anticipating verbs as a result, so the memory cost of long dependencies may play out differently for them.

I should say these individual differences are hard to study well. Experience is tangled up with education, working memory, motivation, and so on. But I think the general picture, that our parsing behavior is shaped by the input we've had, is pretty well supported, and it's also part of why I find comparisons with language models interesting, since they're a very clean case of a system whose behavior is entirely a product of its input.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I find really interesting, partly because it connects to a long-running debate in psycholinguistics about how much of sentence processing is fixed and how much is tuned by experience.

The classic picture from the eighties and nineties was that the parser is more or less a universal module. You have working memory constraints, you have a preference for certain attachment decisions, and those are supposed to be roughly the same whether you read legal contracts all day or mostly text messages. But I think the evidence over the last fifteen or twenty years points pretty strongly in the other direction. People who read a lot, and especially people who read a lot of syntactically demanding material, seem to handle things like center-embedded relative clauses or long-distance dependencies more smoothly. Some of that is just vocabulary and familiarity with the topic, but some of it does look like genuinely better prediction about structure.

The way I'd frame it is that readers are building statistical expectations about what kinds of structures are likely, given what they've seen before. If you've spent years reading German academic prose, where the verb can show up a very long way from the subject, you've learned to hold more material in suspension without panicking. You've also learned which cues are reliable for figuring out where a clause is going to close. Someone who hasn't had that experience isn't necessarily less intelligent, they just haven't had the right training data, so to speak.

What I find appealing about this view is that it fits well with what we see in neural language models. A model trained on a corpus heavy in complex sentences handles complex sentences better, and a model trained mostly on simple text struggles with the same constructions humans find hard. That's not proof that humans work the same way, but it gives us a concrete hypothesis to test, and it lets us ask more precise questions about what exactly experience is contributing. Is it better memory for the specific construction? Is it better strategies for chunking? Is it faster recovery when an initial parse turns out to be wrong? I suspect it's some mixture, and that the mixture differs depending on the construction and the person.

One caveat I'd add is that experience probably doesn't make hard sentences easy. Even expert readers slow down on triple center embeddings. So there seems to be some constraint that experience can push against but not eliminate. Figuring out where that boundary is, and whether it looks the same in humans and in models, is one of the things I'd really like to understand better.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe jumping ahead to a German split verb’s sentence-final portion after encountering its initial portion.

astra-6.text:
I think it can change what you expect a sentence to look like. If you mostly encounter relatively short, simple sentences, then a complicated sentence might lead you down the wrong path: you assume it’s going to end in one way, and then you have to go back and reinterpret it. But if you read a lot of material with elaborate sentence structures, you may become more prepared for those structures and less likely to commit to an interpretation too early.

There are a couple of possibilities there, though. One is that you’re learning the particular patterns that occur in that language or genre. Another is that you’re developing a more general strategy—slowing down, for example, or tolerating uncertainty for longer. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. Getting better at reading a particular kind of complex sentence doesn’t automatically mean you’ll find every kind of complex sentence easier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think your experience can shape what you expect a sentence to look like. If you read a lot of prose with long, complex sentences, you might be more willing to wait for a dependency to be resolved, rather than immediately assuming that you’ve reached the end of a phrase. And you might become better at using the cues that a particular language or genre gives you.

But I’d distinguish expectations from a general ability to process complexity. Being familiar with a construction can make it easier to read without necessarily making you better at every kind of complex sentence. So the interesting question is how specific that adaptation is: are you learning the patterns of a particular author or genre, or does that experience transfer more broadly?
